scenes.visual: Title card 'Why Heat Gives a Peak' fades in over two cartoon bowls of gelatin with pineapple pieces, one wobbly and runny, one firm. THE WORLD, kept for both films: 16:9, warm cream background, flat cartoon shapes, no molecular structures. COLOUR MAP, the same in every scene and in the second film: ENZYME = BLUE rounded block with a notch cut in one side (the notch is the active site), drawn like the lesson's enzyme-cycle figure; SUBSTRATE = ORANGE (a small ORANGE wedge that fits the notch in film 1; ORANGE bead strings for gelatin chains in film 2); PRODUCTS = GREEN; DENATURED ENZYME = GREY bent block whose notch no longer matches the ORANGE shape; WORKING SITES = BLUE counter, top left, reading 'working sites: n of 8'; SPEED PER SITE = YELLOW needle gauge, top right; RATE = PURPLE bar, bottom right, whose height is always the counter times the gauge. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'. ADDED FOR THIS FILM: TEMPERATURE = RED dial with a pointer from 'cold' to 'hot' (no numbers); the BLUE notched block now stands for bromelain.

scenes.tts: Why does fresh pineapple keep gelatin runny, while canned pineapple lets it set? The first film gave us two dials: how many active sites are working, and how fast each one works. Heat turns both of them.
scenes.visual: The two bowls: 'fresh pineapple' runny, 'canned pineapple' firm. A question mark between them. The first film's BLUE counter (top left) and YELLOW gauge (top right) slide in, with the PURPLE rate bar bottom right and the line 'rate = working sites × speed per site'.
scenes.narration: Why does fresh pineapple keep gelatin runny, while canned pineapple lets it set? The first film gave us two dials: how many active sites are working, and how fast each one works. Heat turns both of them.

scenes.tts: Gelatin is a protein. As it cools, its long chains link up into a net that traps water, and the dessert turns firm. Fresh pineapple contains bromelain, really a small family of protein-cutting enzymes. Bromelain cuts the chains, so the net cannot form.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the firm bowl: ORANGE bead strings (gelatin chains) cross and link into a net, holding blue-white water droplets. Cut to the runny bowl: BLUE notched blocks labelled 'bromelain' snip the ORANGE strings into short GREEN pieces, and the net never forms; droplets run free.
scenes.narration: Gelatin is a protein. As it cools, its long chains link up into a net that traps water, and the dessert turns firm. Fresh pineapple contains bromelain, really a small family of protein-cutting enzymes. Bromelain cuts the chains, so the net cannot form.

scenes.tts: So the question is what heat does to bromelain. Hold equal tubes of it at different temperatures, each for the same time. Then compare both dials from tube to tube.
scenes.visual: A row of five test tubes, each with eight BLUE blocks and ORANGE strings and its own small RED temperature dial, pointers stepping from 'cold' (left) to 'hot' (right). A clock icon over the row reads 'same time in every tube'. The camera starts at the cold tube: counter 'working sites: 8 of 8'; YELLOW gauge needle low.
scenes.narration: So the question is what heat does to bromelain. Hold equal tubes of it at different temperatures, each for the same time. Then compare both dials from tube to tube.

scenes.tts: Warmer molecules move faster, so more of them have enough energy to get over the activation-energy hill. The speed of each working site climbs. Up to a point, a warmer reaction runs faster.
scenes.visual: The camera moves tube by tube toward the hot end; in each warmer tube everything jiggles faster. The YELLOW gauge needle rises steadily. A small inset of the first film's hill shows more ORANGE balls crossing. Counter still 'working sites: 8 of 8'. The PURPLE bar rises.
scenes.narration: Warmer molecules move faster, so more of them have enough energy to get over the activation-energy hill. The speed of each working site climbs. Up to a point, a warmer reaction runs faster.

scenes.tts: But a protein enzyme is a folded chain, held in shape by many weak attractions. Too much heat shakes those attractions apart. To denature is for a protein to lose the folded shape it needs to work.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one BLUE block, drawn as a folded ribbon held by small dotted links (no atoms). In the tubes past the middle of the row, the dotted links snap one at a time and the ribbon loosens. The block turns GREY and bends; its notch no longer matches. Label: 'denatured'.
scenes.narration: But a protein enzyme is a folded chain, held in shape by many weak attractions. Too much heat shakes those attractions apart. To denature is for a protein to lose the folded shape it needs to work.

scenes.tts: A denatured enzyme is not dead. It is a molecule whose active site no longer fits. So, in the hotter tubes, the working-sites counter starts to fall.
scenes.visual: Back to the row. In each hotter tube more BLUE blocks are GREY and bent; ORANGE strings bounce off them. The counter reads '8 of 8', '6 of 8', '3 of 8' over successively hotter tubes. The YELLOW gauge keeps rising for the blocks still working.
scenes.narration: A denatured enzyme is not dead. It is a molecule whose active site no longer fits. So, in the hotter tubes, the working-sites counter starts to fall.

scenes.tts: Now multiply the two dials at each temperature. At first the rising speed wins, and the rate climbs. Then the falling counter wins, and the rate drops.
scenes.visual: A graph labelled 'schematic, one test length' draws itself one point per tube, from the cold tube to the hot one (x axis 'temperature, cold to hot', no numbers). A YELLOW dashed curve 'speed per site' rises; a BLUE dashed curve 'working sites' stays flat then falls; the PURPLE solid curve 'rate' is computed as their product at each point (for the animator: speed = exp(0.04·(T−20)), working = 1/(1+exp((T−45)/2.5)) on a hidden 20 to 60 scale; the product peaks near 39). The PURPLE curve is drawn up to and just past its peak.
scenes.narration: Now multiply the two dials at each temperature. At first the rising speed wins, and the rate climbs. Then the falling counter wins, and the rate drops.

scenes.tts: The top of the curve is the optimum, the temperature at which the enzyme works fastest. Above the optimum, the rate often falls because sites are being lost faster than the rest speed up.
scenes.visual: A marker at the PURPLE peak reads 'optimum'. Then a shaded band to the right of the peak is labelled 'losing working sites'; within it small GREY blocks pile up along the BLUE curve. The PURPLE curve slopes down through the band. The word 'often' is underlined in an on-screen caption.
scenes.narration: The top of the curve is the optimum, the temperature at which the enzyme works fastest. Above the optimum, the rate often falls because sites are being lost faster than the rest speed up.

scenes.tts: Back to the pineapple. Canning heats the fruit enough to denature bromelain. The counter falls toward zero. Too little is left to cut the gelatin chains, so they link up into a net, and the gelatin sets.
scenes.visual: A cartoon can of pineapple on a stove, RED pointer swung to 'hot'. Inside, nearly every BLUE block turns GREY. The counter dims to 'working sites: almost none (schematic)'. Cut to the firm bowl: ORANGE strings link into a net, uncut. Label: 'canned: bromelain denatured, gelatin sets'.
scenes.narration: Back to the pineapple. Canning heats the fruit enough to denature bromelain. The counter falls toward zero. Too little is left to cut the gelatin chains, so they link up into a net, and the gelatin sets.

scenes.tts: Now a harder one. Hold fresh pineapple juice as hot as canning does, long enough to denature most of its bromelain. Then cool it and add it to gelatin. Will the gelatin set?
scenes.visual: A glass of fresh pineapple juice is heated (RED pointer to 'hot') and held there while a clock icon runs, then set in a bowl of ice (pointer swings back to 'cold'). It is poured over ORANGE gelatin strings. The counter shows a question mark.
scenes.narration: Now a harder one. Hold fresh pineapple juice as hot as canning does, long enough to denature most of its bromelain. Then cool it and add it to gelatin. Will the gelatin set?

scenes.visual: Hold on the poured juice and the question-marked counter. A 5-second timer ring fills. On-screen text: 'Predict: set or runny?'

scenes.tts: It is likely to set. Cooling does not usually fold the enzyme back up. A few proteins can refold, but heat damage like this is often permanent, like a cooked egg white.
scenes.visual: The gelatin firms up. The counter stays at 'working sites: almost none (schematic)' even as the RED pointer sits at 'cold'; the GREY blocks stay bent. Inset: an egg white turning from clear to white in a pan, then staying white on a cool plate. The words 'likely' and 'often' stay on screen.
scenes.narration: It is likely to set. Cooling does not usually fold the enzyme back up. A few proteins can refold, but heat damage like this is often permanent, like a cooked egg white.

scenes.tts: Heat speeds up each working site, and it can take sites out of work. In this model, the rate peaks at the optimum, where faster sites are offset by lost working sites. Real optima can have other causes, and depend on the test.
scenes.visual: The YELLOW gauge rising and the BLUE counter falling sit on either side of the PURPLE curve's peak. Arrows from each meet at the peak marker 'optimum'. A small caption: 'in this model'. Hold.
scenes.narration: Heat speeds up each working site, and it can take sites out of work. In this model, the rate peaks at the optimum, where faster sites are offset by lost working sites. Real optima can have other causes, and depend on the test.

scenes.visual: End card with the hexagon mascot beside a small PURPLE peaked curve. Line: 'Heat speeds each working site but can remove sites, so rate peaks.'
